memory_candidates.content: When a stub/mock process is invoked inside a bash command substitution `$(cmd 2>&1)` that the calling script never echoes verbatim to its own output (only derives a count/summary from it via e.g. `grep -c`), a test fixture cannot prove 'the guarded/mocked path was taken' by grepping the calling script's own stdout for a marker the mock printed -- the marker is trapped inside the internal capture variable and never surfaces externally, by design (the production script must not leak a raw sub-process log). Prove it indirectly instead: give the mock a distinctive, otherwise-improbable output value (e.g. a sorry-count baked into the stub differing from every other stub also reachable on PATH) and assert the calling script's DERIVED output (the count) reflects that specific value. This also naturally tests that a non-matching noise line (the marker) does not corrupt the substring-based derivation.

When a test fixture must construct a PATH with one specific tool absent (e.g. 'lake' removed) while every other tool the script under test depends on (bash, python3, grep, find, ...) remains available, do NOT strip PATH directories wholesale based on 'does this directory contain the tool to exclude' -- on a NixOS-style system a single directory (e.g. /run/current-system/sw/bin) can resolve MULTIPLE unrelated tools via symlink farm, so blanket removal can silently remove a tool the test still needs (observed: removing the directory containing 'lake' also removed 'bash', breaking every subsequent invocation with 'bash: command not found'). Instead build an isolated bin directory containing only symlinks to the specific tools needed, explicitly excluding the one to omit, and set PATH to just that directory. This is the same technique test-lake-build-guard.sh's own suite already uses (there, to remove systemd-run only) -- reusable as a general PATH-isolation pattern independent of any one suite's naming convention.

When a plan's Verification criteria grep for the literal ABSENCE of specific forbidden substrings (e.g. '8GB', '16GB+', '60-80%') after a documentation rewrite, writing corrected prose that still QUOTES the old claim verbatim to explain what changed ('replaces an earlier claim that memory usage stayed under 8GB...') will fail that grep even though the correction is substantively right -- the literal substring is still present. Rephrase the old claim without the exact forbidden substring (e.g. 'an eight-gigabyte ceiling', 'sixteen-plus gigabyte spikes') while still conveying what was corrected and why.
